hints: Use Pythagoras to find the magnitude $R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$ and trigonometry $\tan\theta = |Y/X|$ to specify the direction clearly relative to one of the given force axes.
walkthrough:
Set up an orthogonal Cartesian coordinate system:
- Positive $x$-axis: horizontal to the right
- Positive $y$-axis: vertical upwards
List the four coplanar forces:
- $60\text{ N}$ force: directed vertically upwards along the positive $y$-axis
- $14\text{ N}$ force: directed horizontally to the left along the negative $x$-axis
- $20\text{ N}$ force: in the first quadrant at $60^\circ$ above the positive $x$-axis
- $16\text{ N}$ force: in the third quadrant at $50^\circ$ below the negative $x$-axis

Resolve all forces along the horizontal $x$-direction:
$$F_x = 20\cos 60^\circ - 14 - 16\cos 50^\circ$$
Calculate each trigonometric component:
$$20\cos 60^\circ = 20(0.5) = 10\text{ N}$$
$$16\cos 50^\circ \approx 16(0.642788) = 10.2846\text{ N}$$
$$F_x = 10 - 14 - 10.2846 = -14.2846\text{ N}$$

Resolve all forces along the vertical $y$-direction:
$$F_y = 60 - 20\sin 60^\circ - 16\sin 50^\circ$$
Calculate each component:
$$20\sin 60^\circ \approx 20(0.866025) = 17.3205\text{ N}$$
$$16\sin 50^\circ \approx 16(0.766044) = 12.2567\text{ N}$$
$$F_y = 60 - 17.3205 - 12.2567 = 30.4228\text{ N}$$

Compute the magnitude of the resultant force $R$ using the Pythagorean theorem:
$$R = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}$$
$$F_x^2 = (-14.2846)^2 \approx 204.050$$
$$F_y^2 = (30.4228)^2 \approx 925.547$$
$$R^2 = 204.050 + 925.547 = 1129.597$$
$$R = \sqrt{1129.597} \approx 33.6095\text{ N}$$
Rounding to 3 significant figures gives $R = 33.6\text{ N}$.

Find the direction of the resultant vector:
Since $F_x < 0$ and $F_y > 0$, the resultant lies in the second quadrant (up and to the left).
Find the acute angle $\theta$ made with the negative $x$-axis (the line of the $14\text{ N}$ force):
$$\tan\theta = \frac{|F_y|}{|F_x|} = \frac{30.4228}{14.2846} \approx 2.12976$$
$$\theta = \tan^{-1}(2.12976) \approx 64.846^\circ$$
Rounding to 1 decimal place gives $64.8^\circ$ above the $14\text{ N}$ force (or an anticlockwise angle of $180^\circ - 64.8^\circ = 115.2^\circ$ from the positive $x$-axis).
